```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(blockr.core)
library(blockr.graph)
```

The package blockr.graph draws a blockr board in the browser as a directed acyclic graph, the DAG.
Each block shows as a node, each link as an arrow from one block to another, and each stack as a box around its blocks.
In the DAG, a user arranges the blocks, links them, adds and removes them, and finds their way around a large board.
This guide is for the people who use the DAG and for those who build apps with it.
It says what the DAG shows, what a user does there, how the DAG places blocks, and what a reader can do on a locked board.
Its last section shows how an app script gives the DAG its state.

## A board in the DAG

This script builds a board of six blocks, three of them in a stack, and serves it:

```{r}
blocks <- c(
  iris = new_dataset_block("iris"),
  head = new_head_block(n = 10L),
  bound = new_rbind_block(),
  bod = new_dataset_block("BOD"),
  cw = new_dataset_block("ChickWeight"),
  joined = new_merge_block("Time")
)

links <- c(
  new_link("iris", "head", "data"),
  new_link("head", "bound", ""),
  new_link("bod", "joined", "x"),
  new_link("cw", "joined", "y")
)

stacks <- c(
  joins = new_stack(c("bod", "cw", "joined"), name = "Joins")
)

serve(new_board(blocks, links, stacks))
```

An app runs every plugin that `available_plugins()` gives, unless its script names the plugins in the `plugins` of `serve()`.
So the DAG runs in every app where blockr.graph is installed.
The page shows the DAG under its name, Workflow.
Under core's basic frontend, the DAG has a section beside the board's blocks, half as tall as the window.
Under blockr.dock, it has a panel of the dock, as every plugin with a UI has.

The script gives the DAG no positions for the blocks.
So the DAG lays the whole board out as it opens, from top to bottom, with the blocks of the stack Joins together in its box.
The last section, [The DAG's state in an app script](#app-script), shows how a script puts the blocks where it wants them.

## What the DAG shows

### Blocks

Each block shows as a node: the block's mark, with the block's name below it.
The mark is the icon of the block's class, on a tint of the colour of the class's category, as on the block's card.

A dot on the lower right corner of the mark shows the block's status, in the colour that the block's card gives the status:

| Status | Dot | Its tooltip |
|---|---|---|
| Ready | Green | Up to date |
| Stale | Grey | Inputs changed since this block last ran |
| Unevaluated | Grey ring | Not evaluated yet |
| Invalid | Amber | Set this block's inputs |
| Waiting | Amber ring | Waiting for a data input |
| Failed | Red | Evaluation failed |

The dot is a ring for a block that has not run yet or that waits for a data input.
So the two grey dots differ by their shape, and so do the two amber ones.
The dot also shows failed where R could not make the block's output, though the block's status is ready.

Small circles on the edges of the mark are the block's handles: one for each data input of the block's class, and one for its result.
A block that takes any number of inputs, as the rbind block does, has a handle for each link into it, and a placeholder for its next input.
A handle sits on the side of the mark that faces the block at the other end of its link.
So a link stays short wherever the user moves either block.
A handle that no link uses sits on the side that the layout's direction gives.
From top to bottom, an input sits on top of the mark, and the result below the block's name.
From left to right, an input sits on the left of the mark, and the result on its right.

While the pointer is over a handle, the handle grows, and a tooltip names it.
It names an input with the block that feeds it, as "data, from Dataset", and names a placeholder "Next input".
Where more handles share a side than fit on it, they crowd together, and they spread out while the pointer is over one of them.

### Links

A link is a curve with an arrow, from the result of the block that it comes from into the input that it feeds.
While the pointer is over a link, the link shows the name of that input.

### Stacks

A stack is a box behind its blocks, in the stack's colour, with the stack's name above it.
A stack that holds no block is a small box with its name and "0 blocks".
A block that the user drops on that box joins the stack.

The button at the top right of a stack's box collapses the stack, and so does a double click on the box.
A collapsed stack shrinks to a small box with its name and the number of its blocks, centred where its box was.
Its blocks hide, with the links between them.
A link between one of its blocks and a block outside the stack ends on the small box.
As the stack collapses, the blocks around it close up on the small box.

The same button, or a double click, expands the stack again.
Its blocks come back where they were, and the blocks around it go back where they were before the stack collapsed.
This holds in whatever order the stacks of a board collapse and expand.
A block that the user moved while the stack was collapsed stays where the user put it, unless it lies in the stack's box, which it then leaves.
Dragging the small box of a collapsed stack moves the stack's hidden blocks with it, so that the stack expands where the box sits.
The board keeps which stacks are collapsed, so a saved board reopens with its stacks as the user left them.

### The empty board

While the board holds no block, the canvas says "No blocks yet. Right-click to add one."

## What a user does in the DAG

Each change that the user makes in the DAG is one step, which the frontend's Undo takes back and its Redo makes again.
The only exceptions are the placement and snapping, which move no block (see [Snapping](#snapping)).
Saving the board keeps what the DAG holds: where each block sits, which stacks are collapsed, and the settings of the layout.

### The view

A drag on the empty canvas pans it, and the mouse wheel zooms it.
The toolbar's Zoom in and Zoom out zoom the canvas too, and its Fit the view shows the whole board.
The DAG fits the view to the board as it first shows a board, at most at full size.
It fits the view again after the user lays the board out again.
It fits the view on no other change, so that the view never moves under the user.
So a block that the user adds elsewhere, as in the Edit board plugin, can land outside the view.
Fit the view then shows it.

While the page stays open, the DAG keeps the zoom and the pan of each board.
So when the dock shows the DAG's panel again, the view is where the user left it.
The board does not keep them, since what one user looks at is no part of the board.

### Selecting

A click selects a block, a link or a stack, and a click on the empty canvas clears the selection.
A click with Cmd on a Mac, or with Ctrl elsewhere, adds to the selection.
A drag on the canvas with Shift held selects what its rectangle covers, with the links between the blocks that it covers.

Selecting one block alone shows the block in the frontend.
Core's basic frontend scrolls to the block's card, and blockr.dock shows the card in the active view.
Selecting several objects, a link or a stack shows nothing.

The DAG shares its selection with the app's other plugins.
So the blocks that the user ticks in the Edit board plugin show as selected in the DAG, and the DAG's toolbar and keys act on them.

### Moving blocks

Dragging a block moves it, and dragging one of several selected blocks moves them all.
Dragging a stack's box moves the stack with its blocks.
A drag selects nothing, so moving a block does not show it in the frontend.
A block that the user drops on the box of another stack joins that stack.
A block that the user drags out of its stack's box stays in the stack, whose box grows to hold it.
Edit stack, in the stack's menu, takes a block out of the stack.
A drag is one step.

The arrow keys move the selected blocks while one of them has the keyboard's focus, by 5 px a press, or 20 px with Shift.
Tab moves the focus from block to block, and Enter or Space selects the block that has the focus.
So the keyboard alone can arrange the board.
A run of presses of the arrow keys is one step, which ends once the user pauses.

### Drawing links

Dragging from the result's handle of one block to an input's handle of another block draws a link.
So does dragging from an input's handle to a result's handle.
A link dropped on a placeholder takes the block's next input.
The DAG checks nothing while the user drags.
Where the board refuses the link, as one that would close a cycle or feed an input that a link feeds already, the DAG draws no link and shows why at the drop.

A link dropped on an empty spot of the canvas adds a block there.
From a result, the drop opens Append block, and from an input, it opens Prepend block.
Each lists the block classes that the user can pick.
The block that the user picks starts at the drop, and a link joins it to the handle where the drag started.
A link dropped on a block or on a stack's box, away from the handles, adds nothing.

### Menus

A right click opens the menu of what lies under the pointer: a block, a link, a stack, an input's handle, or the empty canvas.
Where the object is one of several that the user selected, the menu acts on the whole selection.
So does a right click on the box around a selection.

The menus offer board actions: those of blockr.core, the DAG's own Copy, Cut, Paste and Layout, and those that other packages add.
Every menu of an object offers the same board actions.
So a block's menu in the DAG offers what the menu behind ⋯ on the block's card offers.
In an app of blockr.core and blockr.graph alone, the menus offer these:

| A right click on | Its menu offers |
|---|---|
| A block, or its result's handle | Append block, Create link, Create stack, Rename, Edit inputs, Add to stack, Copy block ID, Copy, Cut and Remove block |
| A link | Insert block, Edit link and Remove link |
| A stack | Rename, Edit stack, Copy, Cut and Remove stack |
| An input's handle | The menu of the link that feeds the input, or where no link does, Prepend block and Create link |
| A selection of several | Create stack, Add to stack, Copy, Cut and Remove |
| The empty canvas | Add block, Create link, Create stack, Layout and Paste |

A menu leaves out a board action that does not apply, as Add to stack on a board without stacks.
A row either runs its board action at once, as Remove block does, or opens the board action's quick action, a short list beside the menu.
The quick action of Append block, for one, lists the block classes that it can add.
What a board action of the canvas's menu adds starts where the user right-clicked.
Where the board refuses what a row asks, the DAG shows why where the user opened the menu.

### Forms below the canvas

Some board actions take a form, as Edit inputs does.
A quick action that has a form offers it through Show all options, the icon at the top right of its list.
The DAG shows such a form in a panel below its canvas.
The canvas shrinks above the panel, and pans where the panel would hide the block, link or stack that the form is about.
The panel closes once the form is done, or as the user presses its Close button or Escape.

The panel's Pin button keeps the panel open once the form is done.
A pinned panel follows the selection.
So as the user selects another block, a pinned Edit inputs shows the inputs of that block.
A pinned Append block moves on to the block that it appended, so that the user can append a chain of blocks.

Where the DAG is narrower than 420 px, or lower than 400 px, the frontend shows the form in its own place instead, as the dock does in its sidebar.

### The toolbar

The toolbar floats in a column at the top left of the canvas.
Each of its buttons has a tooltip that names it.
From the top, it holds:

1. Search blocks, which opens the panel of search and the outline.
2. Zoom in, Zoom out and Fit the view.
3. Add to the board, a + that offers Add block, Create link and Create stack.
4. Paste and Layout.

While the user has selected something, buttons for the selection follow:

5. Add the selection to a stack, a + that offers Create stack and Add to stack.
6. Copy, Cut and Remove.

A block that the toolbar's Add block adds, and a stack that its Create stack adds, start at the middle of the view.
The toolbar shows only what the board offers at the moment, so a button that would offer nothing does not show.

### Search and the outline

Search blocks, the toolbar's first button, opens a panel beside the toolbar.
Its field narrows the panel to the blocks and stacks whose name or ID holds what the user types, the stacks first.

While the field is empty, the panel shows the outline, Board contents.
The outline lists each stack with the number of its blocks, and its blocks in the order of their links, and then the blocks in no stack.
A stack that is collapsed on the canvas shows folded in the outline.
Folding a stack in the outline leaves the canvas alone.

Picking a row moves the view to the block or the stack and selects it.
So picking a block shows the block, as a click on its node does.
Picking a block of a collapsed stack expands the stack first, which moves the blocks around the stack, as every expand does.
Escape, a click outside the panel or a pick closes the panel.

### Copy, cut and paste

Copy puts the blocks and stacks that it acts on onto the clipboard, as a JSON board.
That board holds the blocks of the copied stacks too, the links between the copied blocks, and where each copied block sits.
Cut copies, then removes what it copied, in one step.

Paste adds what the clipboard holds under new IDs, arranged as it was copied.
The blocks keep their names, and the name of each stack gains " (copy)".
The middle of what Paste adds lands where the user opened the menu.
From the toolbar or the key, it lands at the middle of the view.
Where that spot is taken, it lands on the free spot nearest it, so that no other block moves.
A paste is one step.

The clipboard is the system's, so a copy made in another tab or app pastes too.
A browser asks the user before a page reads the clipboard of its own accord, as Paste does from a menu or the toolbar.
Safari and Firefox show a button "Paste" for the user to press, and Chrome asks for a permission.
The key for paste, Cmd+V on macOS and Ctrl+V elsewhere, pastes without asking, since it runs the browser's own paste.
Where the browser does not let the page read the clipboard, Paste takes the last copy made on the page.
Where the clipboard holds no blocks or stacks, Paste adds nothing and says so.
Paste leaves out a block whose class the app does not offer.

### Keys

The DAG's keys act while the keyboard's focus is in the DAG, as after a click on its canvas or on a block.
They never act while the user types in a field, the fields of the DAG's own panels among them.

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| Backspace | Removes the selection |
| Cmd+C on macOS, Ctrl+C elsewhere | Copies the selection, unless the user has selected text, which the browser copies |
| Cmd+X on macOS, Ctrl+X elsewhere | Cuts the selection, unless the user has selected text |
| Cmd+V on macOS, Ctrl+V elsewhere | Pastes |
| The arrow keys | Move the selected blocks while one of them has the focus, by 5 px, or 20 px with Shift |
| Tab | Moves the focus to the next block |
| Enter or Space | Selects the block that has the focus |
| Escape | Closes the panel of a form, unless it is pinned, and takes the block that has the focus out of the selection |

The DAG binds no key for Undo and Redo, which are the frontend's.

Three keys differ from those of blockr.dag, the package that drew the DAG before blockr.graph.
In each, the DAG takes the key of React Flow, the library that draws it.
Users know these keys from other editors built on React Flow:

- Backspace removes the selection, where blockr.dag takes Ctrl with Backspace.
- A drag with Shift held selects by a rectangle, where blockr.dag takes Alt.
- A click with Cmd or Ctrl adds to the selection, where blockr.dag takes Shift.

## How the DAG places blocks

The DAG gives every block a position on the canvas, and the board keeps it.
A block moves only in these cases:

- Someone moves it.
- Someone lays the board out again.
- A stack near it collapses or expands.
- A step adds a block or a stack near it while the placement is Repulsion.

Someone may be the user or the assistant.
The DAG's board action Layout sets how the DAG places blocks.
Its menu opens from the toolbar or from the menu of the empty canvas.

### Placing what a step adds

Whatever a step adds gets its place in the same step, one block or many, whoever adds it.
That may be a menu of the DAG, its toolbar, a paste, another plugin, such as the Edit board plugin, or the assistant.
So one Undo takes back what the step added, with its place, and with what moved to make room for it.

What a step adds starts at a point where the user gives one:

- What the menu of the empty canvas adds starts where the user right-clicked.
- What a link dropped on the canvas adds starts at the drop.
- What the toolbar's Add block and Create stack add starts at the middle of the view.
- What Paste adds starts where the user pasted.

In each case, the DAG puts what the step adds on the free spot nearest the point, with the spacing's gap around it, so that no other block moves.

Otherwise, a block starts by its links, next to the blocks that it is linked to, in the way that their links run:

- A block appended to a block that feeds no other block yet starts one rank past it.
  From top to bottom, that is below it, and from left to right, to its right.
  Where the user has arranged the links into that block another way, the new block follows them.
- A block appended to a block that feeds other blocks already starts one gap past the last of those, level with it.
- A block inserted into a link starts between the link's two blocks.
- A block linked to none starts after the last block of the first rank.
- Several blocks that one step adds start in the order of their links, so that a new chain comes out as a chain.

The placement then fits in what the step adds.
Layout's menu sets it, under New blocks:

- Repulsion, the default, keeps what the step adds where it starts, and moves the blocks around it out of its way.
  The nearest blocks move the most, those further away less, and no two neighbours swap sides.
  So an inserted block stays between its two blocks, and the block that the link fed moves the most.
- Beside moves what the step adds, as a whole, to the nearest free spot, and moves no other block.

As a stack collapses or expands, the DAG moves the blocks around it in the same way: the nearest the most, and no two neighbours swap sides.

### Laying the board out again

Lay out again, in Layout's menu, lays the whole board out, with the direction and the spacing that the menu checks.
Picking another direction or spacing there lays the board out with that one.

- Top to bottom ranks the blocks downwards, so that links run down.
  Left to right ranks them rightwards, so that links run to the right.
- The spacings Compact, Normal and Loose leave gaps of 50, 70 and 100 px between blocks and between ranks.

Each stack keeps its blocks together in its box.
A collapsed stack lays out as its small box, and its blocks keep their places in it.
Laying the board out moves every block, in one step, and the view then fits the board.

The DAG lays the whole board out only when someone asks for it, and as a board opens without positions.
Adding a block never lays the board out.

### Snapping

Snap to grid, in Layout's menu, turns snapping on or off.
While snapping is on, every position that the DAG sets snaps to a multiple of the snap size.
The row Snap size… of the menu sets the snap size, which is 20 px by default.

Turning snapping on moves no block.
A block snaps once something moves it:

- A drag snaps each block that it moves.
- The arrow keys move the selected blocks by the snap size.
- Laying the board out again snaps every block.

Picking a placement and turning snapping on or off move no block.
So Undo skips them: a user who drags a block, then turns snapping on, and then presses Undo takes back the drag.
The board still keeps both settings, and saving the board saves them.

### What each of them cannot do

- Beside moves no other block.
  So on a crowded board, a new block can land further from the blocks that it reads from.
- Making room keeps the arrangement around what it makes room for, but not the ranks of a board that was laid out.
  Laying the board out again restores them.
- Making room keeps every two neighbours in their order.
  So the place of a stack that collapses closes only as far as that lets it.
  The blocks beside a tall stack keep their rows, and leave room above and below its small box.
- A block inserted among blocks lined up a gap apart, as in a column of a board that was laid out, pushes on the blocks lined up beyond it, as far as the line runs.
- Snapping moves a block by up to half the snap size.
  Where that brings a block that the DAG moved closer to another block than the gap, the block moves on to the nearest multiple that keeps the gap.
  A block that the user moves only rounds.
- All of them work from the size that a block's node usually takes, rather than from what the page measures.
  So a long name can still overlap the name of a block beside it.

## On a locked board

An app turns the board lock on with the blockr option `locked`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
options(blockr.locked = TRUE)

serve(new_board(blocks, links, stacks))
```

The board lock fixes the board's blocks, links and stacks.
So in the DAG, a reader draws no link and drops no block into another stack.
The menus and the toolbar leave out every board action that adds, removes or renames a block or a stack, links two blocks, or moves a block into a stack.
Of the DAG's own board actions, Copy and Layout stay, while Cut and Paste go.
On a board without blocks, the canvas says only "No blocks yet."

What the DAG keeps changes how the board shows, never what it computes.
So the DAG locks none of it, and a reader can still explore the board:

- Move blocks, with the pointer or the arrow keys.
- Zoom, pan and fit the view.
- Select blocks, links and stacks.
- Search the board and use its outline.
- Collapse and expand stacks.
- Lay the board out again.
- Copy blocks and stacks.

The load lock and a block's lock change nothing in the DAG.

## The DAG's state in an app script {#app-script}

The board keeps the DAG's state, which holds three things:

- Where each block sits on the canvas.
- Which stacks are collapsed, and where each stack that holds no block sits.
- The settings of the layout.

An app script gives the DAG its state with `new_graph_plugin()`, which it passes in the board's `plugins`:

```{r}
dag <- new_graph_plugin(
  positions = list(
    iris = list(x = 0, y = 0),
    head = list(x = 0, y = 150),
    bound = list(x = 0, y = 300),
    bod = list(x = 300, y = 0),
    cw = list(x = 450, y = 0),
    joined = list(x = 375, y = 150)
  ),
  layout = graph_layout(spacing = "compact", placement = "beside"),
  collapsed = "joins"
)

serve(new_board(blocks, links, stacks, plugins = list(dag)))
```

Each position is the centre of a block's node, which holds its mark and its name below it.
The script gives each position by the block's ID, in pixels of the canvas, with `x` to the right and `y` downwards.
A block is about 50 px across, so a block beside another sits about 150 px from it.
This script puts the chain of `iris`, `head` and `bound` on the left, from top to bottom.
On its right, it puts `bod` and `cw` side by side, with `joined` below them.

Where the script gives some blocks no position, the DAG places those as the board opens, as Beside places what a step adds.
Every other block opens where the script put it.
Where the script gives no position at all, or no DAG plugin, the DAG lays the whole board out as it opens.

The function `graph_layout()` takes the settings of the layout, the same that Layout's menu sets in the app:

- The `direction` is `"TB"`, from top to bottom, the default, or `"LR"`, from left to right.
- The `spacing` is `"normal"`, the default, `"compact"` or `"loose"`.
- The `placement` is `"repulsion"`, the default, or `"beside"`.
- The flag `snap` says whether positions snap, and is `FALSE` by default.
- The `snap_size` is the snap size in pixels, 20 by default.

The direction and the spacing move no block until the DAG lays the board out, as it opens without positions or as someone lays it out again.
The direction also gives the side of a handle that no link uses, and the way that a new block starts where no link shows the way.

The argument `collapsed` names the stacks that the board opens with collapsed, by their IDs.
Expanding such a stack moves only the blocks in the way of its box, since nothing moved as it collapsed.
The function `plugin_state()` of blockr.core gives the state that the plugin holds:

```{r}
str(plugin_state(dag), max.level = 2)
```

The constructor takes no position for a stack.
The DAG places each stack that holds no block as the board opens.

The constructor checks the shape of what it is given, but knows nothing of the board.
So a position or a collapsed stack that names a block or a stack that the board lacks reaches the browser.
The DAG drops such an entry as the board opens, and names it in a warning, which the frontend shows.

A script that names the plugins in the `plugins` of `serve()` has to name the DAG among them, by its id `graph_plugin`.
This app runs core's basic frontend and the DAG, and no other plugin:

```{r}
plugins <- available_plugins()
plugins <- plugins[plugins$id %in% c("basic_frontend_plugin", "graph_plugin"), ]

serve(new_board(blocks, links, stacks, plugins = list(dag)), plugins = plugins)
```
